sentences.text: You know, since the dawn of humanity, we have always been fascinated by our bodies.
You can go back to cave paintings or the Dark Ages where people's skulls were being cut open to explore, to today where we're constantly trying to understand ourselves.
And yet people might be surprised at how little we still know about the human body.
As much as we know, it continues to expose our ignorance.
As soon as you learn something, two more questions arise or three more questions arise.
You know, science can sometimes be reductionistic, but the reality is everything you change in the body has compounding effects in other areas of the body.
Here at Nike, we're about pushing the limits of what people think is humanly possible.
We're still understanding the limits of human endeavors and what it means to be a human in motion.
My name is Matthew Nurse.
I'm the Chief Science Officer here at Nike, and I have the privilege of working with an amazing team in the Nike Sport Research Lab.
I got to Nike by way of academia, like the way most scientists learn their craft.
I've been here for 23 years.
I didn't have aspirations when I was young of working in a shoe company per se, but I always had a love of medicine and biology and medical science with engineering and sport.
And so when you get to this place and you see it and you experience it, it's hard to say no.
Nike was founded on this notion of if you have a body you're an athlete, and when I first got here it was very much, how do we make footwear and apparel that helps athletes be better?
Initially this lab and a lot of other labs like it tended to be really focused on, what do humans or athletes do to product?
But over time, we started to shift that conversation away from not just what do humans do to our products or athletes do to our products, but what do our products actually do to athletes?
How do our products make them better?
And that was a fundamental shift for us about 15 years ago, and it really accelerated sort of the pace and scale of both the research but the innovation here.
The beauty of the body is there's always another problem, there's always another challenge, there's always another version of human potential that has yet to be solved.
And so it's really rare that we start with a product as the opportunity.
We don't think about what's the next shoe.
We think about fatigue.
We think about performance.
We think about injury.
We think about confidence.
You have to always look at it through a multidimensional lens.
You know, when we think about the scientific method, it's a process for uncovering new truths.
It's a process for expanding innovation.
Everything we do in the Sport Research Lab, we try and understand athletes.
We capture data, whether that's movement data, whether that's physiological, whether it's neurological, or even just spoken word.
How do we do it in a way that we can quantify it?
And if you can measure it, you know, as the saying goes, you can improve it.
One of the things I'm really obsessed with right now is injuries, and particularly in female athletes.
Women are at a higher risk of ACL injuries than men.
They're three to five times more likely to have an injury.
ACL injuries are multifactorial.
Particularly in female athletes, people have looked at the bone structure around the knee.
They've looked at how changes in a woman's hormonal fluctuations might change the laxity of the ligaments in the knee, all the way down to sort of just motor patterns and motor development.
We have historically treated young boys and young girls differently, and how we let them move as infants can have an impact on how they move and develop as they get older.
And so solving those big challenges, if you solve for her, you'll solve for everybody.

If we think about how we look at science at Nike through a biomechanics lens, which is studying the movement and the loads on the body, we look at it through a physiology lens, sort of your body's internal regulatory mechanisms and how do you respond to different stimuli.
We look at it through perception and neuroscience lens.
You can't just look at one thing in isolation and assume you understand the full picture.
One of my favorite examples of this one is a sports bra.
When a woman puts on a sports bra, the first thing that she experiences is she has a greater thermal load.
She has more layers on, sweat is less likely to evaporate, and she retains heat more than her male counterparts.
And so every woman is at a disadvantage on the starting line.
We call it the bra tax, for wearing a bra.
At the same time, we know if we change a woman's support, she will move either consciously or subconsciously differently.
Women tend to brace. They might hunch over.
Not only does that make the movement less efficient, it might expose you to greater injury risks.

And so we're constantly looking at what are the acute changes that happen with these different interventions, different products and services, but also what are those long-term impacts so that you can be the best version tomorrow and the day after and the year after going forward.
Part of being a great scientist is also being really creative.
The most enduring impact that a science team or the Nike Sport Research Lab can have is the ability, the capacity, the creativity to imagine a different future that doesn't yet exist.
The folklore of a two-hour marathon had been around for years and was largely seen as impossible.
When we did the work leading up to Breaking2, we didn't start and say, let's run a two-hour marathon.
We actually started with fatigue.
Every single person on the planet gets fatigued.
Some do it while they're doing a two-hour marathon, some just navigating the streets of their urban community.
And so what that made us think about was, how do you define fatigue?
Is it muscular?
Is it neuromotor?
Is it physiological?
And then you start from there building the knowledge and basically putting the ingredients on the table.
We knew that if you change mass by roughly 100 grams in a shoe, you start to change running economy by about 1%.
We also knew if you change cushioning, you can also affect running economy by about 1%.
And we knew if you change plate stiffness, you can change run economy by 1%.
Now, we were trying to see how do we combine cushioning, plate stiffness, and weight to help reduce fatigue.
A lot of times in science, what we have found is when you try and combine all three of those effects, the 1 plus 1 plus 1 rarely equals 3.
It probably equals 2.
And one of the things we found almost unexpectedly was it was 4%.
Just by putting on a shoe, you were 4% more efficient at running.
When I first saw those results, I told my team they had done it wrong and they needed to go back and try again because it almost never works out that way.

And so sometimes you get these magical moments where when you start to look at systems and you start to look at the whole body as opposed to individual levers, you get these compounding benefits and/or unanticipated outcomes.

If you look at what the marathon time of the day was, and we look at the benefit we were both getting from what we thought we could do in training and modeling athlete performance, along with the products that we were showing would give you a 4% benefit,
all of a sudden it felt that the two-hour marathon was within grasp, and from there I'd say the rest is history.
As a, maybe as a pragmatist and a scientist, sometimes I think we're reaching an asymptote.
And then something magical happens.
There's a breakthrough that changes performance.
These technological breakthroughs change our perception, our reality.
One of the amazing things and very unique to humans is our ability to expand our potential through innovation and technology and science.

If you think about how writing changed how we preserve memories, if you think about how the printing press changed how we disseminate knowledge, you think about GPS and how it changed how we navigate the world, it's extended our reality.
And so as we put different things on you, we change the way you move, we change the way you experience the world, we change the way you're able to train and adapt and respond.
And, you know, that's the beauty of the human system.
When we study these people, every single person has something deeply, deeply amazing about them.
And we have so much opportunity still and so much room to grow.
Science is never done.
It's not infallible.
It's the best truth that we have today.
But one of the hallmarks of science, too, is you share your findings.
This is what we think.
This is what we built.
This is what we think it does.
I welcome the feedback.
Please tell me I'm wrong.
And let's build on that knowledge and go out and solve these problems together.
And so just living to the virtues of good science and debate and sharing, and I think that's how we move the world forward.
